diagnostic_evidence.quote: From the physical point of view, imposing an artificial potential in the fluid context is equivalent to generating a desired pressure.
The pressure $p$ is determined by the divergence-free (volume-preserving) constraint $\hbox{div}\,v=0$.
we can distinguish at least one direction along which the fluid accelerates towards the obstacle

issues.failure_explanation: For phi in Diff_vol(Omega) (unit Jacobian, bijective), int_Omega V(phi(x))dx = int_Omega V(y)dy, independent of phi and v. The potential term in the cost is therefore a constant and cannot change the minimizers. Equivalently, admissible variations are delta phi = w∘phi with div w = 0 and w tangent to the boundary. Then <grad V∘phi, delta phi> = <grad V, w> = 0, so the V-force cannot appear in the extremal equations. The proof of th1 treats delta phi as unconstrained although the space of curves requires phi(.,t) in Diff_vol. Th2's equation is just Euler's equation with pressure p-V. The paper itself says p is fixed by div v=0, so v is exactly the V=0 solution and the pressure cannot be 'desired'. The paper claims V makes the fluid avoid the obstacle, but nothing supports this, and its own description of the simulation shows fluid accelerating toward the obstacle.

failure_location.quote: we show how the artificial potential can help the fluid avoid a circular obstacle located at a single point, for which no physical barrier exists

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, the formulation must be changed so the potential acts on the dynamics in a way not absorbed by the incompressibility pressure (e.g. a non-gradient or density-dependent force, or relaxing volume preservation), and the results and simulations must be redone.
issues.overall_effect: The central motivation (a modified Euler flow that avoids obstacles via an artificial potential/pressure) is unsupported. Th1/th2 remain formally derivable but carry no V-dependent content. The simulation cannot demonstrate avoidance.
issues.title: Artificial potential cannot influence the incompressible flow, so the 'desired pressure' and 'obstacle avoidance' claims are vacuous
issues.why_classification: Every resolution needs a different problem formulation and new derivations, and the advertised obstacle-avoidance conclusion is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: the tangencial component of $v$ vanishes at the boundary
which are parallel to the boundary

issues.failure_explanation: The integration by parts leaves the boundary term int_{dOmega} k delta v . n dS. Vanishing requires delta v . n = 0 on the boundary. The assumption in Section 2.1 only says the tangential component of v vanishes, which gives no information on the normal component. The Lie-algebra description says the opposite (fields parallel to the boundary). The proof instead invokes 'v vanishes on the boundary', a third condition, and cites v rather than the variation delta v whose trace matters. The claim that the stated assumption is the minimal requirement for Stokes' theorem is incorrect.

failure_location.quote: where the last term vanishes since $v(x,t)$ vanishes on $\partial\Omega$ and we deduce that

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State one consistent boundary condition (v and delta v tangent to the boundary, or fully vanishing) in Sections 2.1, 2.4 and in the space of curves, and invoke delta v . n = 0 in the proof.
issues.overall_effect: As written, the k-equation v = pi∘phi^{-1} - grad k, and hence th2, is not justified under the stated boundary assumption.
issues.title: Boundary term in the proof of Theorem 1 justified by a hypothesis that is inconsistent with the stated assumption
issues.why_classification: A local, routine hypothesis correction restores the argument without changing the method or conclusions.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof's last variational identity has the coefficient of delta phi equal to (Tv∘phi)^T pi + d_t pi + grad V∘phi = 0, which gives d_t pi = -(Tv∘phi)^T pi - grad V∘phi. The proof concludes +grad V∘phi, so the sign flips at the last step. Separately, the extended functional J carries -1/2<v,v> + V∘phi, i.e. it encodes the cost 1/2<v,v> - V, whereas the stated problem has cost 1/2<v,v> + V. So J does not correspond to the optimal control problem. Depending on which sign is kept, Theorem 2 should read -grad(p+V) or -grad(p-V), and the two choices have opposite repulsive/attractive meaning.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Make J consistent with the stated cost (use -V in J, or change the cost to 1/2<v,v> - V) and correct the sign in the final display, then restate th1/th2 accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The sign of the V-force in th1 and th2 is not established by the stated functional, so the direction of the modified Euler force is unreliable.
issues.title: Sign of the potential term is inconsistent between the cost, the extended functional, and the conclusion of Theorem 1
issues.why_classification: A local sign correction in J or the conclusion, consistent through the proof, restores the derivation with the same method.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The potential function $V$ is an artificial smooth (or at least $C^{2}$) potential function
decays to zero at some positive level set far away from the obstacle $S$

issues.failure_explanation: V = 1/f (e.g. tau/(rho^2 - r^2)) is singular on S inside Omega and changes sign across S, so it is not C^2 on Omega. Near rho = r it behaves like tau/(2r(rho-r)), which is not integrable, so int_Omega V∘phi dx = int_Omega V dx diverges or is undefined for volume-preserving phi. grad V∘phi is undefined where phi maps points into S. Th1/th2 use int V∘phi and grad V∘phi and require V smooth, so they do not apply to the potentials the paper proposes and simulates. V = tau/(rho^2 - r^2) vanishes only at infinity, not on a finite level set, and the claim that this 'ensures' trajectories avoid S is given without any argument.

failure_location.quote: To avoid collision with obstacles we introduce a potential function $V$ defined as the inverse value of the function $f$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use a smooth bounded (e.g. compactly supported) barrier V on Omega, or restrict to potentials with an integrable singularity and prove the needed regularity. Drop the unsupported 'ensures no intersection' and 'decays to zero at a level set' statements.
issues.overall_effect: The application of th1/th2 to the stated obstacle potentials (the paper's motivating use case and simulation) is unjustified.
issues.title: Proposed obstacle potentials are singular on S inside Omega, contradicting the regularity the results need
issues.why_classification: The theorems stand for smooth V, but obstacle-type barriers need a contained modification and a weakened claim, not new global architecture.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: even though we depart from divergence-free initial conditions

issues.failure_explanation: For u = -sin y cos x and v = sin y cos x, div = d_x u + d_y v = sin x sin y + cos x cos y = cos(x-y), which is not identically zero. The paper nevertheless states that the simulation departs from divergence-free data. The stated initial field violates the incompressibility constraint of the model, and the correct field is not determined by the text.

failure_location.quote: using as initial conditions the functions $u(x,y,0) = - \sin y \cos x$ and $v(x,y,0)= \sin y \cos x$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the initial field with a divergence-free one (e.g. a Taylor–Green-type field) or explicitly project the initial data, and rerun or re-describe the simulation.
issues.overall_effect: The reported simulation does not start from an admissible incompressible state as claimed, so its description is unreliable.
issues.title: Simulation initial data are not divergence-free although described as such
issues.why_classification: A local correction of the initial data or an initial projection restores consistency without changing any claim or method.
